a1.title: Pay for Lunch With a Recipe
a1.excerpt: At one small café, you can pay for lunch with a family recipe.
a1.body:
Hana is a cook. She has a small café by the sea.

Every Wednesday, people do not pay with money. They pay with a recipe! They write a family recipe on a card. Then they eat lunch.

Every Friday, Hana cooks one recipe. The writer's name is on the menu.

Now Hana has 800 recipes. The favourite is a pancake recipe. It is from a boy. He is eight.

Hana loves the recipes. “They tell me about my town,” she says.

a2.title: A Café Where You Can Pay With a Recipe
a2.excerpt: Every Wednesday, a small harbour café takes family recipes instead of money, and it now has 800 of them.
a2.body:
Hana is 39. She opened a small café near the harbour three years ago.

Last year, she started a new idea. On Wednesdays, customers can pay for lunch with a family recipe. They don't pay any money. They write the recipe on a card and give it to Hana.

Every Friday, Hana chooses one recipe and cooks it. She writes the name of the person on the menu board. People love to see their family's food at the café.

After one year, Hana has 800 recipes. They come from families with roots in more than 40 countries.

The most popular dish is a potato pancake. An eight-year-old boy sent the recipe. On his card, he wrote: “My dad's pancakes, but better.”

Hana put 100 recipes in a cookbook. The money from the book pays for free cooking lessons for teenagers.

vocab.definition: a place where boats stay, near the land

b1.title: The Harbour Café Where Lunch Costs One Family Recipe
b1.excerpt: Every Wednesday, customers at a small harbour café pay for lunch with a handwritten family recipe — and the chef has now collected 800 of them.
b1.body:
On most days, the small café by the harbour works like any other: you order, you eat, you pay. But on Wednesdays, the chef doesn't want your money. She wants your grandmother's secrets.

Hana Morrow, 39, opened the café three years ago. Last year, she started an experiment: on Wednesdays, customers could pay for lunch with a family recipe instead of cash. All they had to do was write it down on a card and sign their name.

“I expected maybe ten recipes,” Hana says. “By the end of the first month, I had two hundred.”

Every Friday, she picks one of the cards and cooks it as the “Recipe of the Week”, with the writer's name on the menu board. Many people come back on Friday just to see their family's dish being served to strangers.

A year later, Hana has collected 800 recipes from families with roots in more than 40 countries. The most popular so far is a potato pancake, sent in by an eight-year-old boy. His card said simply: “My dad's pancakes, but better.”

Hana has put a hundred of the recipes into a cookbook. The money it makes pays for free cooking lessons for local teenagers.

“Money pays the bills,” Hana says. “Recipes tell me who my neighbours really are.”

b2.title: No Cash Needed: The Harbour Café Where Lunch Is Paid For in Family Recipes
b2.excerpt: A chef's small Wednesday experiment — lunch in exchange for a handwritten family recipe — has produced 800 cards, a community cookbook and a long table full of strangers swapping stories about their grandmothers.
b2.body:
There is a small café by the harbour where, one day a week, money is politely refused. On Wednesdays, the only accepted form of payment is a family recipe, handwritten on a card and signed by its owner.

The idea came from Hana Morrow, a 39-year-old chef who opened the café three years ago. She had noticed that customers loved to tell her about the dishes they had grown up with, but that very few of those recipes had ever been written down. “So many of them only existed in someone's head,” she said. “I thought, if I don't ask for them now, they might disappear.”

The experiment was supposed to last a month. Hana admitted that she had been expecting perhaps a dozen cards; by the end of the first four weeks, she had received more than two hundred. A year later, the collection stands at 800 recipes, contributed by families with roots in over 40 countries.

Every Friday, one card is chosen at random and cooked as the Recipe of the Week, with its author's name chalked proudly on the menu board. Many contributors turn up specifically to watch strangers eating their family's food, and some bring relatives along to taste the result.

Lunch is served at a single long table, which has turned out to be half the point. “People who would never normally have spoken end up comparing notes on how their grandmothers made dumplings,” one regular observed.

The runaway favourite so far is a humble potato pancake, submitted by an eight-year-old boy. His card, now framed above the counter, reads in full: “My dad's pancakes, but better.” His father, Hana reports, has taken the comment in good spirit.

A hundred of the recipes have since been gathered into a community cookbook, and every penny it earns is used to fund free cooking lessons for local teenagers.

Asked whether the Wednesday arrangement makes financial sense, Hana laughs. “If I only cared about money, I would have stopped after a week,” she says. “Money pays the bills. Recipes tell me who my neighbours really are.”

c1.title: Settled in Secrets: The Harbour Café That Accepts Family Recipes Instead of Cash
c1.excerpt: What began as a month-long experiment in a small harbour café has become an archive of 800 handwritten family recipes, a community cookbook and, perhaps unexpectedly, one of the town's most reliable places to make friends.
c1.body:
There is a café by the harbour where, every Wednesday, the till remains firmly shut. On that day, lunch cannot be bought — at least not with money. The only currency accepted is a family recipe, written out by hand on a postcard-sized card and signed by the person who knows it best.

The scheme is the creation of Hana Morrow, a 39-year-old chef who opened the café three years ago and soon noticed a curious pattern. Customers would linger at the counter to describe, often in elaborate detail, the dishes they had grown up eating, yet almost none of those recipes had ever been committed to paper. “They lived in people's hands and in their memories,” she says. “It struck me that, unless someone asked, a great many of them would simply vanish.”

Her solution was intended as a modest, month-long experiment. She anticipated perhaps a dozen contributions; within four weeks she had received well over two hundred. A year on, the archive stands at 800 recipes, submitted by families whose roots stretch across more than 40 countries, and it shows no sign of slowing.

Every Friday, a card is drawn at random from a battered biscuit tin and cooked as the Recipe of the Week, its author's name chalked on the menu board with due ceremony. The ritual has acquired a following of its own. Contributors routinely turn up to watch, with a mixture of pride and anxiety, as strangers taste their family's cooking for the first time; some arrive with three generations in tow.

Behind the counter, the cards themselves are treated with something approaching reverence. Each is photographed, catalogued by region and main ingredient, and filed in a row of wooden drawers rescued from a closed-down sewing shop. Some are written in careful capitals; others arrive splattered with sauce, annotated in two or three languages, or accompanied by small sketches explaining exactly how a dough should be folded. Hana has resisted every suggestion to tidy them up. “The stains are part of the recipe,” she insists.

Lunch is served at a single long table, and it is there, arguably, that the project's real value lies. Conversations that would otherwise never have taken place unfold over shared plates, as retired dockworkers and university students compare notes on the correct thickness of a dumpling or the precise moment to add the garlic. “You come for the food,” one regular observes, “and leave knowing half the street.”

Not every recipe is a treasured heirloom. The runaway favourite to date is a humble potato pancake submitted by an eight-year-old boy, whose card — now framed and hung above the counter — reads, in its entirety: “My dad's pancakes, but better.” His father, Hana reports diplomatically, has accepted the verdict with good grace.

A hundred of the recipes have since been compiled into a community cookbook, the proceeds of which fund free weekly cooking classes for local teenagers — many of whom, fittingly, have begun contributing recipes of their own. The classes, held on Monday evenings when the café is otherwise closed, are taught by the very people who submitted the recipes, so that a retired sailor might spend an evening demonstrating his mother's fish stew to a room of politely sceptical sixteen-year-olds.

Whether the Wednesday arrangement makes commercial sense is a question Hana has clearly been asked before. “Were I running this place purely for profit, I'd have abandoned the idea after a week,” she says, with a shrug. “But money only pays the bills. Recipes tell me who my neighbours really are.”
